what: Real User Monitoring (RUM) collects performance numbers from the browsers of actual visitors, using the web-vitals library or PerformanceObserver, and sends them to your backend with sendBeacon. It shows what real devices and networks experience, which lab tests can't.
like: Like asking every diner to fill in a tiny rating card as they leave, instead of only tasting the food yourself in the kitchen.
why: Shows real p75 and p95 across devices, networks and countries
Catches regressions after a deploy that lab tests missed
Points at the exact element or interaction that was slow

steps.d: Import onLCP, onINP and onCLS from the web-vitals library (about 3 KB brotli). It handles the tricky rules (bfcache restores, hidden tabs, iframes) on top of PerformanceObserver.
Observe largest-contentful-paint, layout-shift, longtask, event and navigation entries with buffered: true to get entries recorded before your script ran. Check supportedEntryTypes first.
The attribution build (about 1.5 KB more) tells you which element, URL or interaction caused the number, so you can act on it.
Send when the page becomes hidden (visibilitychange), not on unload, using navigator.sendBeacon, with fetch keepalive as fallback. Keep each payload small (beacon limit is 64 KiB).
Save metric, value, id, route, device class, connection, country and release version so you can slice later. Sample if traffic is large.
Chart p75 (the pass/fail line) and watch p90 or p95 for the slow tail. Avoid averages. Alert when p75 crosses a threshold after a release.

numbers.l: web-vitals library size, brotli'd; the attribution build adds about 1.5 KB
Total size limit of queued sendBeacon data
CrUX is a 28-day rolling aggregate of real Chrome users - your own RUM can be more current and per-user
Report the 75th percentile for pass/fail and watch higher percentiles for slow users; avoid averages

tool: web-vitals, PerformanceObserver, CrUX, Vercel Speed Insights, Datadog RUM, OpenTelemetry

choices.d: A small collector plus web-vitals is cheap and gives full control. Vendors (Datadog, Sentry, Vercel Speed Insights, SpeedCurve and others) add dashboards, sessions and alerts.
CrUX is free and is what Google uses, but it is Chrome-only, aggregated and lagging. Own RUM covers all browsers, works per route and release, and is near real time.
Sample a percentage on high-traffic sites. Keep dimension cardinality low (route templates, not full URLs) so storage stays cheap.
Send performance numbers, not personal data. Avoid full URLs with IDs or query strings, and respect consent rules.

instead.why: Defines the metrics and thresholds RUM reports against
Can buffer beacons offline, though sendBeacon already queues for you

breaks.d: Data is sent on unload, which doesn't fire reliably (especially mobile).
breaks.see: Missing CLS or INP values; undercount
breaks.fix: Send on visibilitychange hidden with sendBeacon

breaks.d: Averages hide the slow tail and outliers.
breaks.see: Mean looks fine while users complain
breaks.fix: Use p75 and p95 by segment

breaks.d: Releases aren't tagged, so a regression can't be tied to a change.
breaks.see: Metric dips with no known cause
breaks.fix: Tag every beacon with a release version and compare before and after

say: I'd use the web-vitals library with attribution, send on visibilitychange with sendBeacon, and store route, device, connection and release as dimensions.
I read p75 as the pass line and p95 for the slow tail, never averages, and alert when p75 regresses after a release.
CrUX tells me how Chrome users experience the origin; my own RUM covers every browser and lets me slice by route.

followups.a: Lighthouse is one device, one network and one run. It can't capture real interactions, so it can't predict INP, and it misses variation by device, country and cache state.

followups.q: How do you keep RUM from hurting performance?
followups.a: The library is tiny, send work is deferred to idle or page hide, payloads are small, and you sample on high traffic. The collector must never block the page.

today: The web-vitals library (with its attribution build) over PerformanceObserver is the standard approach, CrUX supplies Google's reference data, and most monitoring vendors build on the same APIs. The practice is to segment by route, device and release and to tie every metric to its likely cause.

sources.t: web.dev: Lab and field data differences

check.q: When should metrics be sent so they are not lost?
check.a: When the page becomes hidden (visibilitychange), via sendBeacon
check.why: visibilitychange is reliable, unload is not, and sendBeacon survives page exit.

check.q: Which statistic should you chart for Core Web Vitals pass/fail?
check.why: p75 is the pass/fail line; averages hide outliers and the slow tail.

check.q: What does PerformanceObserver's buffered: true do?
check.a: Delivers entries recorded before observe() was called
check.why: Without it you would miss early entries like LCP candidates.
